title: CAN A CHRISTIAN BELONG TO JESUS… AND STILL BE UNDER SPIRITUAL ATTACK?
paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN BELONG TO JESUS… AND STILL BE UNDER SPIRITUAL ATTACK?
The terrifying battle many believers fight in silence—and the biblical truth that changes everything about fear, oppression, and the authority of Jesus Christ.
She loved Jesus.
That was the part nobody understood.
She prayed before going to sleep. She listened to worship music while washing the dishes. She highlighted Bible verses about peace, deliverance, and the promises of God.
She believed Christ had saved her.
Yet some nights, when the house became quiet and everyone else was sleeping, she would lie awake with a heaviness she couldn't explain.
Fear that seemed to come from nowhere.
Accusations that replayed old mistakes.
Thoughts that whispered she wasn't really forgiven.
And sometimes, a terrifying question would rise from somewhere deep inside her:
If I really belong to Jesus, why does it still feel like darkness is fighting for me?
She didn't tell anyone.
Because Christians were supposed to have victory.
Weren't they?
Christians were supposed to have peace.
Weren't they?
And if she admitted what was happening, perhaps someone would tell her she lacked faith. Or worse, that something evil had taken possession of her.
So she kept smiling at church.
Kept singing.
Kept serving.
Kept answering, "I'm blessed," whenever someone asked how she was doing.
But inside, she was exhausted.
Maybe her story sounds uncomfortably familiar.
Maybe you've prayed and still felt afraid.
Maybe you've surrendered your life to Christ, yet your mind sometimes feels like a battlefield.
Maybe you've wondered whether recurring temptation, intrusive thoughts, nightmares, spiritual dryness, or overwhelming discouragement means the enemy has somehow gained ownership over your life.
And maybe the question you've been too ashamed to ask is the very question we need to answer honestly:
Can a Christian be spiritually oppressed while genuinely belonging to Jesus Christ?
The biblical answer is both sobering and extraordinarily hopeful.
Yes, believers can experience spiritual opposition, temptation, harassment, and attacks from the devil. But spiritual opposition is not the same as spiritual ownership.
And that distinction may be one of the most important truths you will ever understand.
Because the enemy may fight against someone who belongs to Christ.
But fighting against someone is not the same as possessing them.
Let that settle in your heart.
The battle may be real.
But so is the Savior.
And Scripture never tells the Christian to measure Christ's ownership by how peaceful the battlefield feels.
It tells us to look at the One who purchased us with His blood.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"Ye are bought with a price."
—1 Corinthians 6:20, KJV
In the original Greek, the expression is:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
Ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
"For you were bought with a price."
The verb ēgorasthēte expresses the reality of having been purchased. In Paul's argument, believers are not their own; they belong to God and must glorify Him with their bodies.
This isn't a poetic slogan.
It is the foundation of Christian identity.
If you are genuinely united to Jesus Christ through faith, your deepest identity is not defined by your worst temptation, darkest season, most frightening thought, or most painful struggle.
You belong to the Lord who redeemed you.
And no spiritual attack can overturn the finished work of Calvary.
But that doesn't mean the Christian life is free from conflict.
In fact, the Bible tells us the opposite.
Peter wrote to believers:
"Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour."
—1 Peter 5:8, KJV
Notice something that is easy to overlook.
Peter was addressing Christians.
People who had been called by God.
People who possessed a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And yet he warned them to remain spiritually alert.
The Greek word translated "adversary" is ἀντίδικος (antidikos), a term associated with an opponent or legal adversary.
Peter describes the devil as an enemy who actively opposes God's people.
But Peter does not tell Christians to surrender to terror.
The very next verse says:
"Whom resist stedfast in the faith."
—1 Peter 5:9, KJV
Resist.
Not panic.
Not obsess over demons.
Not assume every hardship is a curse.
Resist, standing firm in the faith.
The Bible acknowledges the enemy's opposition without ever making the enemy the center of the believer's life.
That place belongs to Jesus.
And if we are going to understand spiritual oppression biblically, we must begin there.
Because some believers have been taught to fear Satan more than they trust Christ.
Every nightmare becomes a demon.
Every illness becomes a curse.
Every anxious thought becomes evidence of an evil presence.
Every closed door becomes spiritual warfare.
But Scripture does not authorize us to make those automatic conclusions.
The Bible speaks clearly about spiritual warfare, but it also speaks about human weakness, suffering, grief, bodily illness, sinful desires, persecution, and the burdens of living in a fallen world.
Not every painful experience has the same cause.
And faithful Christians must be careful not to claim supernatural knowledge that God has not given them.
Consider Job.
He was described as upright and God-fearing.
Yet suffering devastated his life.
He lost his children, his possessions, his health, and the comfort he once knew.
The opening chapters of Job reveal a spiritual dimension to his suffering that Job himself could not see.
But notice the devastating mistake his friends made.
They believed they could explain his suffering with certainty.
They assumed his pain must expose hidden wrongdoing.
They spoke confidently where they should have spoken humbly.
And God eventually rebuked them for failing to speak rightly about Him.
There is a warning here for the modern church.
When a struggling believer comes to us trembling, we should not immediately declare, "You have a demon."
We should not automatically accuse them of secret sin.
We should not turn every unexplained experience into a dramatic deliverance story.
Sometimes the most Christlike thing we can do is sit beside a hurting person, listen carefully, pray sincerely, and refuse to add shame to their suffering.
Because suffering is not proof that Jesus has abandoned someone.
And spiritual warfare is not evidence that salvation has failed.
Think about the apostle Paul.
He knew what it meant to suffer while belonging completely to Christ.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7, Paul described a "thorn in the flesh" as:
"the messenger of Satan to buffet me."
The Greek phrase includes:
ἄγγελος Σατανᾶ
Angelos Satana.
Literally, "a messenger of Satan."

The exact nature of Paul's thorn remains debated among biblical interpreters. Scripture does not identify it with enough precision for us to declare whether it was a particular illness, a hostile opponent, or another affliction.
But one truth is unmistakable.
Paul was suffering.
Paul was praying.
Paul was a servant of Jesus Christ.
And the Lord did not tell him that the suffering proved he belonged to Satan.
Instead, Christ answered:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
—2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Imagine that.
Paul asked for the affliction to depart.
Three times.
And Jesus answered by revealing the sufficiency of His grace.
Not because Paul's suffering was insignificant.
Not because his pain was imaginary.
But because the presence of suffering did not mean the absence of Christ's sustaining power.
Somebody reading this has been begging God to remove a burden.
You've prayed until you ran out of words.
You've wondered why the struggle continues.
And perhaps you've begun to believe that your unanswered prayer means God is disappointed in you.
But Paul's testimony confronts that conclusion.
Sometimes the Lord delivers us from an affliction.
Sometimes He sustains us through an affliction.
And His sustaining grace is not a lesser expression of His faithfulness.
A battle that continues is not necessarily a battle that Christ has abandoned.
Now we must address a distinction that has caused enormous confusion.
Can a Christian be demon-possessed?
The New Testament frequently uses the Greek verb δαιμονίζομαι (daimonizomai) for people afflicted by demonic activity. English translations often render it "demon-possessed" or "demonized."
The Greek term describes demonic affliction, but by itself it does not settle every modern theological question about ownership, indwelling, or the precise degree of demonic influence.
That matters.
Because Christians sometimes build elaborate teachings on English terminology without examining what the biblical texts actually establish.
Scripture clearly teaches that believers can be tempted, deceived, accused, opposed, and spiritually attacked.

But the Bible does not provide an explicit, unambiguous example of a genuinely regenerate, Spirit-indwelt Christian being owned or inhabited by a demon in the same sense described in the Gospel accounts of demonic affliction.

Christians from different traditions disagree about whether a believer can experience some form of internal demonic affliction. Those disagreements should be approached with humility rather than sensationalism.
What Scripture does clearly teach is that those who belong to Christ have been transferred out of the dominion of darkness.
Colossians 1:13 declares:
"Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son."
The Greek expression for "power of darkness" includes:
ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους
Exousias tou skotous.
The word exousia can refer to authority, jurisdiction, or dominion.
Paul's point is magnificent.
God has rescued His people from the authority of darkness and brought them into the kingdom of His beloved Son.
This is not merely a promise of future rescue.
It describes a decisive saving action accomplished by God.
The Christian's spiritual citizenship has changed.
Their ultimate allegiance has changed.
Their Lord has changed.
And the devil has no authority to reverse what God has accomplished through the redemption of Jesus Christ.
This does not make believers invulnerable to temptation or suffering.
It means the enemy is not their rightful master.
Remember that distinction.
Because the devil's strategy often involves making Christians forget what God has already declared.
He accuses.
He tempts.
He deceives.
He seeks opportunities to exploit spiritual carelessness.
But he cannot become the Savior, Judge, or rightful owner of those whom Christ has redeemed.
And perhaps nowhere is the tenderness of that truth more visible than in the story of Peter.
On the night before Jesus was crucified, Peter believed he was stronger than he really was.
He was confident.
Passionate.
Certain that he would never deny his Lord.
Then Jesus spoke words that must have shaken him.
"Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat."
—Luke 22:31, KJV
In Greek, Jesus said:
Σίμων Σίμων, ἰδοὺ ὁ Σατανᾶς ἐξῃτήσατο ὑμᾶς τοῦ σινιάσαι ὡς τὸν σῖτον
Simōn Simōn, idou ho Satanas exētēsato hymas tou siniasai hōs ton siton.
The plural pronoun hymas indicates that the warning extended beyond Peter alone to the disciples.
Satan sought to sift them like wheat.
To shake them.
To test them.
To expose their weakness.
But listen to what Jesus said next.
"But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not."
—Luke 22:32, KJV
There it is.
The enemy wanted to sift Peter.
But Jesus was interceding for Peter.
And those are not equal powers competing for control.
Jesus already knew Peter would deny Him.
He knew the rooster would crow.
He knew Peter would weep bitterly.
He knew the shame that would follow.
Yet Jesus did not discard Peter.
He prayed for him.
And He spoke of Peter's future restoration.
"When thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren."
In this context, "converted" refers to Peter turning back, not necessarily to receiving initial salvation.
Jesus was looking beyond the collapse.
Beyond the denial.
Beyond the tears.
Beyond the night Peter would wish he could erase.
And after the resurrection, beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Read John 21:15–19.
The man who denied Jesus three times was not beyond the restoring grace of Jesus.
What a Savior.
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
His restoration was not cheap.
But his story did not end in the courtyard of denial.
It continued in the mercy of the risen Christ.
And maybe that is what someone needs to hear today.
You fell.
You compromised.
You said something you wish you could take back.
You returned to a temptation you promised God you would never entertain again.
Now shame is telling you that your failure has the final word.
But shame is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
And repentance is not running away from Him because you are ashamed.
Repentance is turning back to the One whose mercy is greater than your excuses and whose holiness is greater than your sin.
This is not permission to continue in disobedience.
Grace never makes sin harmless.
It makes restoration possible through the crucified and risen Christ.
The same Jesus who forgives sinners also calls them to follow Him.
And genuine faith does not make peace with the darkness Christ died to rescue us from.
Paul wrote in Ephesians 6:11:
"Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil."
The Greek word translated "wiles" is μεθοδείας (methodeias), referring to schemes or crafty methods.
Notice that Paul does not tell believers to discover secret demonic names, reconstruct ancestral histories, or live in constant fear of invisible enemies.
He tells them to put on God's armor.
Truth.
Righteousness.
Readiness rooted in the gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The Word of God.
Prayer.
These are not theatrical accessories.
They describe a life of dependence on God, shaped by His truth and sustained through faith.
And the command repeated throughout this passage is striking.
Stand.
Stand firm.
Withstand.
Not because the Christian possesses independent supernatural greatness.
But because the Christian stands in the strength of the Lord.
"Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might."
—Ephesians 6:10, KJV
The Christian's confidence is not that the enemy is weak. It is that Jesus Christ is Lord.
And there is another truth we cannot afford to ignore.
Some believers are so frightened of spiritual oppression that they begin interpreting their own mental suffering as proof of demonic activity.
An intrusive thought appears, and they panic.
A frightening dream occurs, and they assume a spirit has entered their home.
They experience anxiety, depression, trauma symptoms, sleep paralysis, or other distressing experiences, and someone tells them that seeking medical care would demonstrate a lack of faith.
Please hear this carefully.
That is not a conclusion Scripture requires.
Mental health struggles are not automatic evidence of demonic oppression.
Neither are intrusive thoughts, panic attacks, chronic illness, or nightmares.
Such experiences can have psychological, neurological, physical, environmental, or other causes.
They deserve careful attention rather than careless spiritual labeling.
Prayer and appropriate medical or mental health care are not enemies.
A Christian may seek help from qualified professionals while continuing to trust God, study Scripture, and receive compassionate support from a faithful church community.
And if someone is experiencing voices commanding harm, severe confusion, or an immediate danger to themselves or others, urgent professional help is appropriate.
We must never use the language of spiritual warfare to delay necessary care.
Jesus never commanded His people to abandon wisdom.
Nor did He call His church to humiliate the suffering.
He calls us to love one another.
To bear one another's burdens.
To speak truth.
To pray.
To exercise discernment.
And to remember that the suffering person in front of us is not a spectacle.
They are a human being made in the image of God.
Sometimes the most powerful ministry in a room is not the loudest prayer.
It is the believer who stays.
Who listens.
Who refuses to condemn.
Who opens Scripture gently.
Who helps someone find the care they need.
Who reminds a frightened soul that they are not alone.
And who points them back to Jesus without pretending to know everything about their pain.
But what if the struggle really does involve spiritual temptation, deception, or opposition?
What should a Christian do?
James 4:7 gives an answer that is remarkably clear.
"Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."
In Greek:
Ὑποτάγητε οὖν τῷ θεῷ· ἀντίστητε δὲ τῷ διαβόλῳ
Hypotagēte oun tō theō; antistēte de tō diabolō.
"Therefore submit yourselves to God; but resist the devil."
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
The first movement is surrender to the Lord.
Not obsession with the enemy.
Not a frantic attempt to discover whether every hardship has a demonic explanation.
Submission to God.
Confession of known sin.
Trust in Christ.
Obedience to His Word.
Dependence on His grace.
And resistance to the devil's lies.
When temptation says, "Nobody will know," remember that God sees and calls you into the light.
When condemnation says, "Your sin is too great," remember that Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for those who come to Him in faith.
When pride says, "You don't need accountability," remember that Christians are called to encourage and strengthen one another.
When fear says, "You are completely abandoned," remember the promise of Jesus:
"I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee."
—Hebrews 13:5, KJV
And when shame says, "You can never come back," remember the father in Luke 15 running to receive his returning son.
But don't confuse resisting the devil with pretending sin has no consequences.
If you have been living in deliberate rebellion, don't cover it with religious language.
Repent.
If you've been nurturing bitterness, bring it before God.
If you're trapped in a pattern of deceit, seek truth and accountability.
If you are hiding destructive behavior, stop protecting the darkness.
The gospel offers forgiveness, but it also calls us into a transformed life.
Jesus does not merely comfort us in our chains.
He calls us to follow Him into freedom.
And sometimes the first act of spiritual courage is not shouting at the devil.
It is finally telling the truth.
"I need help."
"I have been hiding."
"I am struggling with temptation."
"I have been afraid."
"I need to repent."
"I don't know how to carry this anymore."
Those words may feel humiliating.
But bringing a struggle into the light can be the beginning of healing.
And if you're reading this with tears in your eyes, perhaps because you have been carrying a secret battle for months or years, I want you to remember something.
Jesus already knows.
Not merely the polished version of you.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the person who knows when to raise their hands during worship.
He knows the exhausted person who sits in the car after church, unable to explain why they still feel empty.
He knows the person who keeps opening the same Bible passage because they desperately want to believe the promise applies to them.
He knows the person who has been afraid to confess a recurring sin.
He knows the believer who feels spiritually numb.
He knows the wounded soul who is tired of hearing simplistic answers to complicated pain.
And He is not confused by your weakness.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that Jesus is a High Priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
Then the next verse invites believers to approach the throne of grace boldly, to receive mercy and find grace for help in time of need.
Do you see the beauty of that?
The Bible does not tell struggling believers to hide until they become worthy of approaching God.
It tells them to approach through Jesus Christ.
Because our confidence is not in the perfection of our performance.
It is in the sufficiency of our High Priest.
And His name is Jesus.
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who confronted the powers of darkness.
The One who healed the afflicted.
The One who welcomed sinners.
The One who was betrayed, mocked, scourged, and crucified.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose from the dead.
And the One who now intercedes for those who draw near to God through Him.
At the cross, evil did its worst.
Human betrayal.
Religious hypocrisy.
Political injustice.
Cruelty.
Shame.
Death.
Everything seemed to be collapsing into darkness.
But the cross was not Satan's victory.
It was the place where the Son of God gave Himself for our redemption.
Colossians 2:15 declares that Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them.
The victory belongs to Jesus.
And the empty tomb announces that death itself could not hold Him.
This is why the Christian message is not simply, "Fight harder."
It is, "Look to Christ."
Trust His finished work.
Repent of your sins.
Believe the gospel.
Walk in obedience.
Remain in His Word.
Pray without ceasing.
Stay connected to the body of Christ.
And when you fall, do not make your failure your permanent address.
Return to the Savior.
Because the Christian life is not a story about how powerful we are against darkness.
It is a testimony to how gracious and mighty Jesus is toward sinners He redeems.
And perhaps the most beautiful reminder comes from Romans 8.
Paul asks:
"Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?"
He names tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, and sword.
He doesn't pretend suffering is imaginary.
He doesn't promise believers an effortless life.
He looks directly at the terrifying realities of human existence and declares that none of them can separate God's people from His love in Christ Jesus.
Then he writes:
And the passage concludes:
"Nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
—Romans 8:38–39, KJV
Read that again.
Not even powers.
Not even the terrifying things you cannot fully understand.
Not even the suffering you wish would disappear.
For those who truly belong to Christ, God's saving love is not fragile.
It does not evaporate every time fear rises.
It does not disappear because temptation knocks.
It is grounded in Jesus Christ our Lord.
This is not a promise that every person who merely claims Christianity is automatically saved regardless of faith or repentance.
It is the glorious assurance of those who belong to Christ through genuine faith.
And if you are uncertain where you stand with God, the answer is not to become consumed with analyzing demons.
The answer is to come to Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Receive His grace through faith.
Follow Him.
Because salvation is not found in winning a supernatural guessing game.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
Maybe today is the day you stop asking only, "Why is the enemy fighting me?"
And begin asking a deeper question.
"Lord Jesus, how do You want me to respond faithfully in this season?"
Maybe the answer will involve repentance.
Maybe it will involve forgiveness.
Maybe it will involve reaching out to a trusted pastor.
Maybe it will involve getting professional help for a burden you have carried too long.
Maybe it will involve rebuilding habits of prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and honest accountability.
Maybe it will involve finally believing that your past does not have greater authority than the gospel.
Whatever the next faithful step is, take it with your eyes on Christ.
Not because you can control every battle.
But because you know the One who holds you.
And if you have spent years believing that being attacked means being abandoned, hear this:
The presence of a battle does not cancel the promise of the Savior.
You can be weary and still belong to Jesus.
You can be tempted and still resist through His grace.
You can be wounded and still be loved.
You can be suffering and still be held.
You can have a history you deeply regret and still discover that repentance and forgiveness are real.
Your story may contain scandal.
Your past may contain shame.
Your present may contain struggles nobody sees.
But Jesus Christ is able to redeem what sin has ruined and transform those who turn to Him in faith.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because pain was imaginary.
Not because our stories were always beautiful.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
But by making redemption greater than the shame that once defined us.
And I want to ask you something personal.
If you've been fighting a battle in silence, what would it mean to stop pretending you have everything together?
You don't need to reveal private details or expose wounds you aren't ready to share.
Your words might encourage another believer who is struggling to hold on.
Someone reading may need to know that spiritual maturity does not mean never struggling.
It means learning to trust, obey, and return to Christ in the middle of the struggle.
And perhaps this message wasn't meant to stop with you.
Think of the friend who has grown quiet.
The family member who used to be passionate about God but now seems spiritually exhausted.
The believer who is afraid to admit what they're facing.
The person who has mistaken depression for divine rejection.
The seeker who believes their past is too dark for grace.
Not merely to circulate another religious post, but because biblical truth can bring clarity where fear has taken root.
Because discipleship is not supposed to end when a Sunday service finishes.
We need the Word of God on ordinary Mondays.
During difficult conversations.
During temptation.
During seasons of grief.
During the long, quiet hours when nobody knows how hard we are fighting to remain faithful.
Our desire is to help believers move beyond momentary inspiration into a deeper understanding of Scripture, a stronger walk with Jesus, and a life increasingly shaped by His truth.
And if this ministry has encouraged you, challenged you, or helped you return to God's Word, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Not because giving money makes God love you more.
The gospel is never for sale.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price for our redemption, and salvation is received by grace through faith, not purchased through financial contributions.
But Scripture does teach the beauty of willing generosity in supporting faithful ministry.
Paul wrote:
"God loveth a cheerful giver."
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The same verse teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion.
That matters deeply to us.
We want it to come from a heart that loves Jesus and genuinely desires to help make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
Think about what that means.
More Scripture-centered articles reaching people who are spiritually exhausted.
More accessible discipleship resources.
More opportunities to encourage believers who are struggling.
More content that points beyond religious performance to the finished work of Jesus Christ.
More reminders that repentance is possible, grace is real, and nobody is beyond the reach of the Savior.
It is a voluntary partnership in a mission that seeks to glorify Him.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read.
Still learn.
Still pray.
Still grow.
Still invite others.
Your worth before God is not measured by your ability to give money.
And a struggling believer should never feel that financial hardship places them outside the reach of Christian encouragement.
What matters most is that Jesus Christ is glorified and His gospel is faithfully proclaimed.
Because at the end of the day, this ministry is not about building a following around a personality.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
The Savior who confronted darkness without fearing it.
The Savior who restored Peter after his denial.
The Savior who sustained Paul in weakness.
The Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
The Savior who still invites the weary to come to Him.
And if you are that weary person today, I want to leave you with a simple prayer.

Lord Jesus, I confess that sometimes my fears feel greater than my faith. Sometimes I don't understand the battles I face, and sometimes I have allowed shame to silence me. Forgive my sins. Expose the lies I have believed. Teach me to submit to You, resist temptation, and stand firmly in Your truth. Give me wisdom to seek the help I need, courage to confess what must be confessed, and humility to walk with Your people. Remind me that my hope is not in my strength but in Your finished work. Guard my heart, renew my mind, and lead me in obedience. Above everything else, let my life glorify You. In Your holy name, Jesus. Amen.
The one lying awake in the darkness.
The one who loved Jesus but feared that her struggles meant she had lost Him.
Imagine her opening her Bible to John 10.
Imagine her reading the words of Jesus:
"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
Then a few lines later:
"Neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand."
—John 10:27–28, KJV
Her circumstances may not change overnight.
She may still need prayer, counsel, medical care, rest, repentance, or patient support.
But one truth can begin to change how she faces the darkness.
She does not have to interpret every frightening feeling as evidence that Jesus has let go.
She can return to His promises.
She can seek help without shame.
She can resist temptation without surrendering to despair.
She can follow the Shepherd who knows His sheep.
And perhaps tonight, for the first time in a long time, she can whisper something different.
Not, "Why am I so weak?"
Not, "Has God forgotten me?"
Not, "Does darkness own me?"
But this:
"Jesus, I am Yours. Help me trust You, even here."
And that is where I want to leave you.
Not staring at the darkness.
But looking to the Savior.
The enemy may remind you of the night you fell, but Jesus still calls repentant sinners to rise and follow Him into the light.
